facts.fact_text: On 5 December 2011 the applicants took part in a public demonstration (a meeting) at Chistyye Prudy, Moscow.
The demonstration on 5 December 2011 had been duly authorised by the mayor of Moscow.
The meeting on 5 December 2011 was conducted by the second applicant.
During the meeting on 5 December 2011, the first applicant addressed the participants with a speech calling for fresh, fair elections.
During the meeting on 5 December 2011, the first applicant described United Russia, the election frontrunner, as "a party of crooks and thieves".
The applicants claimed that at the end of the meeting they had headed, with other people, towards the Kuznetskiy Most metro station, where the first applicant had left his car.
The applicants claimed that they were walking along the pavement, leaving the road clear for traffic.
The applicants claimed that their way was suddenly blocked by the riot police (сотрудники внутренних войск и ОМОН).
The applicants claimed that without any introduction or demand, the police surrounded a group of about one hundred protesters, including the applicants, pressing them against a building.
The applicants claimed that the surrounded group chanted "One for all, and all for one!".
After the demonstration on 5 December 2011, the applicants were arrested.
The applicants claimed that their way was suddenly blocked by the riot police (сотрудники внутренних войск и ОМОН).
The applicants claimed that without any introduction or demand, the police surrounded a group of about one hundred protesters, including the applicants, pressing them against a building.
The applicants claimed that the surrounded group chanted "One for all, and all for one!".
The applicants claimed that the riot police then began to arrest the protesters.
Both applicants were arrested at about 8.45 p.m. on 5 December 2011.
Both applicants were taken to a police bus after their arrest.
At about 9.40 p.m. on 5 December 2011 the applicants were taken to the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station, Moscow.
At 11.40 p.m. on 5 December 2011 the first applicant was subjected to a body search at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station, which lasted until 12.15 a.m.
The applicants were unable to retrieve the seized objects, although those objects were not attached to the case file.
The applicants requested that their lawyers, who had arrived at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station and had presented their authority, be allowed to see them.
The applicants' request to see their lawyers at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station was refused.
The applicants were not allowed to make a phone call to their families at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station.
At the Vostochnyy District police station the applicants requested to see a lawyer and to make a phone call, but this was refused.
The first applicant lodged a complaint about the refusal to see a lawyer and make a phone call at the Vostochnyy District police station.
At 2.30 a.m. on 6 December 2011 the applicants were transferred to the Kitay-Gorod District police station.

At the Kitay-Gorod District police station, police reports were drawn up stating that the applicants had been escorted to the police station in accordance with Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

At 2.40 a.m. on 6 December 2011 further police reports were drawn up at the Kitay-Gorod District police station in which it was decided to remand the applicants in custody under Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The applicants were charged with an administrative offence for refusing to comply with a lawful order of the police, in breach of Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The applicants claimed that the conditions of detention during their transfer between the police stations were inhuman and degrading.
The applicants claimed that the conditions of detention in the cell at the Kitay-Gorod District police station were inhuman and degrading.
The applicants claimed that they had spent six hours being driven to different police stations without being given any food or drinking water.

The applicants claimed that at the Kitay-Gorod District police station they were placed together in a cell measuring about 6 sq. m with concrete walls, a metal grill, a concrete floor, no windows and no furniture except for two narrow wooden benches.
The applicants claimed that the cell at the Kitay-Gorod District police station was poorly lit and had no ventilation.
The applicants claimed that there was no sanitary equipment, beds or bedding in the cell at the Kitay-Gorod District police station.

The applicants claimed that they did not receive any food or water until later on 6 December 2011 when they were allowed to receive a parcel from their families containing drinking water and crackers.
The applicants claimed that no food other than drinking water and crackers was allowed in the parcels from their families.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001, at the material time, provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of their official duties related to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the performance by them of their official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between 500 and 1,000 Russian roubles or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 27.2(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the escorting or the transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative offence report, if this cannot be done at the place where the offence was discovered and if the drawing up of a report is mandatory, shall be carried out by the police.
Article 27.2(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the escort operation shall be carried out as quickly as possible.

Article 27.2(3) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the escort operation shall be recorded in an escort operation report, an administrative offence report or an administrative detention report, and that the escorted person shall be given a copy of the escort operation report if he or she so requests.

Article 27.3(3) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that where the detained person so requests, his family, the administrative department at his place of work or study and his defence counsel shall be informed of his whereabouts.

Article 27.3(5) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the detained person shall have his rights and obligations under the Code explained to him, and the corresponding entry shall be made in the administrative arrest report.

Article 27.5(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the duration of administrative detention shall not exceed three hours, except in the cases set out in paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Article.

Article 27.5(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences involving unlawful crossing of the Russian border may be subject to administrative detention for up to 48 hours.

Article 27.5(3) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences punishable, among other administrative sanctions, by administrative detention may be subject to administrative detention for up to 48 hours.

Article 27.5(4) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the term of the administrative detention is calculated from the time when a person escorted in accordance with Article 27.2 is taken to the police station, and in respect of a person in a state of alcoholic intoxication, from the time of his sobering up.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided, at the material time, that a public event could be stopped if there was a real threat to life or the physical integrity of persons or property.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided, at the material time, that a public event could be stopped if the participants had acted unlawfully or the event organiser had knowingly breached the requirements of the Act as regards the conduct of the event (section 16).

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), a representative of the public authority, who had to be present at the event, could order the event organiser to put an end to the event in circumstances justifying stopping the event.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the representative of the public authority had to explain the reasons for the order to end the event and provide time for compliance with it.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), if the organiser did not comply with the order to end the event, the public official could issue the same order to the participants.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), if both the organiser and participants failed to comply with the order to end the event, the police were to take appropriate measures to stop the event (section 17).

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held in the first applicant's case that the Justice of the Peace had correctly established that the first applicant had disobeyed a lawful order of a police officer.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that at 8.45 p.m. on 5 December 2011 at 2 Teatralnyy Proyezd, Moscow (near Metropol hotel), after the authorised public meeting at Chistoprudnyy Boulevard, the first applicant participated with a group of about 60 people in a march that had not been notified to the executive authorities.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the first applicant went out on the road and continued walking from Chistoprudnyy Boulevard, down the side streets to Bolshaya Lubyanka Street, Kuznetskiy Most Street, and Rozhdestvenka Street in the direction of Red Square.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the first applicant obstructed the traffic and created a risk of accident while shouting out "Shame!", "This is our city!", "Russia without Putin!", "Down with the police state!".

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that a police cordon was set up at the crossroads of Pushechnaya and Rozhdestvenka Streets to intercept the march, and that repeated lawful orders to stop and end the march were given through a loudspeaker.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that despite the police orders, the first applicant with a group of people pushed through the cordon and came out onto Teatralnyy Proyezd while continuing to chant slogans, where they were met by another police cordon.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the first applicant did not react to the repeated lawful orders to stop and disperse, continued his unlawful acts drawing the attention of citizens and the press.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that during his arrest the first applicant, in reply to an invitation to proceed to the police bus for the issuing of an administrative offence report, began to push away police officers I. and F., trying to cause panic among people, thereby manifesting his refusal to comply with the lawful orders of the police and preventing them from carrying out their duties, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

In their appeals, the applicants complained of unlawful detention during the first six hours after their arrest.
In their appeals, the applicants complained of lack of access to a lawyer.
In their appeals, the applicants complained of the conditions in which they had been transferred between the police stations and remanded in custody at the Kitay-Gorod District police station.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the complaints about the refusals to hear witnesses and to admit the evidence requested by the applicants.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow rejected the applicants' requests to have witnesses called in the appeal proceedings.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow rejected the request to admit the video recordings in evidence because of their "unknown provenance".
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow refused to keep a verbatim record of the hearing because it considered it unnecessary.
On 7 December 2011 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the applicants' appeals and upheld the first-instance judgment in both cases, citing the same reasons.

During the appeal hearing in the first applicant's case, the second applicant was examined as a witness and testified that at the time of the first applicant's arrest he had been with him at Teatralnaya Square.

The second applicant testified as a witness in the appeal hearing that at the time of arrest they were on the pavement near the underpass and did not commit any unlawful acts, and that about 100 people were blocked by the riot police.

The second applicant testified as a witness in the appeal hearing that both the first applicant and the second applicant were arrested virtually simultaneously, that the police officers did not give any orders, there was no disobedience on the part of the applicants, and that police officers I. and F. did not take part in their arrest and their court testimonies were false.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow found the second applicant's witness testimony unreliable and dismissed it because it contradicted the testimonies of police officers I. and F., which were described as logical, consistent, concordant and objectively corroborated by the written evidence.
The first applicant requested that two video recordings of his arrest, shot by witnesses T. and A., be admitted as evidence in the administrative proceedings.
The first applicant requested that the court obtain and examine the video footage which the police had at their disposal.

The requests to admit the video recordings were dismissed on the grounds that the court had no technical means of playing the recordings and that it would be unacceptable to use the devices provided by the defence.
The requests to admit the video recordings were not joined to the case file on the grounds that they had been submitted at the wrong stage of the proceedings.
